transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-18
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Liu (Redwood SE), Ellen Park (Pacifica CTO), Diego Ramos (Lead ML), Priya Singh (Security)
Links shared: https://files.redwood.ai/pacifica/host-compare.xlsx (Jordan), https://files.redwood.ai/pacifica/benchmark-plan.md (Maya)

Auto-summary (auto): Quick scoping to decide pilot hosting mode (hosted vs dedicated vs private/VPC), agree success criteria (latency, cost per 1k tokens, availability), define benchmark matrix and schedule pilot window. Discussed compliance constraints (SOC2, KMS, data residency) and expected workload shapes (burst QPS vs steady).

Topics: success criteria, workload sizing, bench matrix, timelines, private deployment concerns, warmup/cold cache, fallback policies

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking time. Quick intro from our side, I'm Jordan AE and with me is Maya, our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Ellen (CTO): Hi, Ellen here. Thanks. We wanted to run through hosting tradeoffs. Our main ask is a 90-day pilot to decide final deployment.
[00:20] Maya (SE): great; we'll cover success metrics and propose a benchmark plan. Diego, could you start with current infra and traffic profile?
[00:28] Diego (Lead ML): Yeah, sure. So as background, we process sensor telemetry, mostly short messages but occasionally long context windows for anomaly triage. Typical steady QPS is 25 rps, peak bursts up to 250 rps for 30-90s during fleet events. Latency target for interactive triage is 200ms p95 if possible, but we'll tolerate up to 350ms for some flows. Cost is big for us, we have to keep per-inference spend under $0.03 per call on average.
[00:55] Priya (Security): For us, SOC2 compliance and key separation are blockers for hosted unless we have customer-managed KMS and audit logs. Also data residency - EU telemetry must stay in EU region.
[01:10] Jordan: Got it, thanks. To frame tradeoffs quickly: Hosted (Redwood API) gives fastest time-to-value with our managed model catalog, transparent per-token pricing, and streaming. Dedicated is reserved capacity with predictable throughput and isolation, and Private/VPC gives you a control plane in your VPC or on-prem for strict compliance. We'll propose a matrix.
[01:36] Ellen: We listed three hypothesis: 1) hosted will be cheaper to start, 2) dedicated lowers unit cost at scale, 3) private is necessary only if our compliance team says so. We need data to validate.
[01:47] Maya: Perfect. For the pilot we recommend three buckets: latency benchmark, throughput burn, and failover/availability. Latency bench should capture cold starts, warm steady-state, and tail p95/p99. Throughput bench to emulate your 250 rps bursts and sustained 25 rps. Also memory/KV cache behavior for long-context calls.
[02:08] Diego: Can you explain what KV cache means in practice? I see it in the docs but not sure how it affects latency.
[02:15] Maya: Sure. KV cache is the model's key-value cache for attention states; efficient KV handling avoids recomputing earlier tokens so long-chat-like flows get much faster second and subsequent calls. On Redwood Dedicated and Private, we can pin a session across GPUs to keep KV warm which reduces tail latency. On hosted we have prefix caching and session affinity but warm state policies vary depending on load and tenant isolation.
[02:44] Ellen: Any quantization differences? We run some smaller models already.
[02:48] Maya: We can serve quantized variants (4-bit/8-bit) across all modes; dedicated/private often let you pick specialized kernels that improve throughput further. But quality regressions are a factor to include in success criteria. We'll include response-quality checks in the bench.
[03:05] Jordan: On cost modeling, we'll provide a spreadsheet comparing per-token hosted pricing, committed capacity tiers for Dedicated, and an estimate for Private (including infra hours, egress, and ops lead time).
[03:16] Diego: Important: during those 30-90s bursts we care about tail-latency and warm-cache. If a hosted pool multiplexes too aggressively, we might see increased p95.
[03:27] Maya: That's a real tradeoff. For Dedicated you get a GPU pool per customer so you can control batching windows; for hosted we rely on continuous batching with tenant isolation. We'll simulate your burst pattern in the benchmark so we can measure this concretely.
[03:40] Priya: On the security side, what audit logs do you expose with hosted? Does it include token-level usage and request bodies? We cannot expose raw telemetry to a managed service.
[03:50] Jordan: Hosted includes token-level cost and latency breakdowns and standard request metadata, but not raw payloads unless you opt in. For regulated flows we recommend Redwood Private with a customer-managed control plane and KMS/HSM integration. We can provide SOC2 artifacts either way.
[04:07] Ellen: Timeline wise we're aiming to choose by mid-June and have production by Q3. Pilot needs to finish by June 5th. Is that realistic?
[04:16] Maya: We can target a 3-day bench window week of May 25th, then analyze, then a 2-week POC for integration. To finish by June 5th is tight but feasible if we lock access and share prompts by May 20th.
[04:29] Diego: We'll need scripts to replay traffic, and keys for private endpoints if we test VPC. Also a sample prompt set with edge cases.
[04:36] Jordan: We'll share: benchmark-plan.md (Maya) and host-compare.xlsx (Jordan). We'll need volume estimates (qps histogram) and sample payloads.
[04:46] Ellen: On success criteria, we propose: 1) p95 latency <= 250ms for common flows, 2) total cost delta vs baseline < 10% for 6 months, 3) no compliance red flags (SOC2/KMS) for Private option.
[04:58] Maya: We'll add quality criteria: top-line accuracy/regression < 2% vs your golden set for sampled prompts. Also availability SLO of 99.9% during pilot window.
[05:09] Diego: For workload sizing, what does dedicated capacity commit look like? We have variable peaks.
[05:15] Jordan: Dedicated reserves GPU pools. We'll propose a commit level to cover steady-state plus headroom for expected bursts; there's also burst capacity options. We'll model cost tradeoffs in the spreadsheet. Typically customers with sustained high QPS and stringent tail-latency prefer Dedicated.
[05:30] Priya: If we go Private on-prem, lead time? Our infra team will need deployment scripts and an air-gapped package.
[05:36] Maya: Private on-prem lead time depends on your infra team bandwidth, usually 4-8 weeks for full on-prem with KMS integrations, shorter for VPC deployments (2-4 weeks). We can do a hybrid: run benchmarks on Redwood Dedicated hosted GPUs but validate integration with your VPC for compliance review.
[05:54] Ellen: Regarding data residency, can you guarantee EU-only hosting for the pilot?
[05:58] Jordan: Yes, we can pin the pilot to EU region for hosted and Dedicated; Private/VPC would be within your region by definition. We'll note that in the plan.
[06:07] Diego: Bench specifics: for long-context runs we need 2x tokens (1k and 4k) to see effect on KV cache and quantization. Also measure memory pressure and OOM risks.
[06:18] Maya: We'll include 512, 1024, and 4096 token runs and measure p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec. Also cold-starts: run a cold restart sequence and measure first-request latencies.
[06:31] Jordan: For next steps recap: Jordan shares cost matrix and region constraints, Maya shares bench plan and will propose test harness and sample prompts, Pacifica will supply qps histogram and sample payloads. We'll schedule bench window week of May 25th.
[06:46] Ellen: Sounds good. One more: our procurement team wants competitor pricing references; Anthropic and OpenAI are being evaluated.
[06:53] Jordan: Understood. We'll include comparative notes (public pricing) but note differences in exact feature parity.
[06:59] Diego: Anything about fallback policies? If we go dedicated and saturate, how are requests routed to hosted?
[07:05] Maya: We can configure smart routing and automatic fallback to a compatible model variant on hosted or lower-tier dedicated pool. Fallback policy is part of deployment config. We'll show examples.
[07:17] Priya: For audit purposes, include list of logs exported and retention TTLs.
[07:22] Jordan: We'll include an audit artifact list.
[07:25] Ellen: Great. If we confirm prompts by May 20th, you can run bench week of 25th, deliver analysis by May 28th?
[07:33] Maya: Yes, we aim to deliver initial bench analysis by the 28th and a recommendation with cost model by May 30th.
[07:40] Jordan: Final note - we'll try to simulate your bursts with the client's replay harness; Diego, can you share the replay tool and S3 location?
[07:47] Diego: Yes, I'll share S3 link and replay scripts by tomorrow.
[07:50] Speaker 1 (misc): uh yeah, and we'll also include a small smoke test for on-prem installs.
[07:55] Jordan: Thanks all. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the bench window.

Closing recap (auto): Pilot plan agreed: 3-day bench + 2-week integration POC; success criteria defined (latency, cost, compliance, quality); deliverables and owners assigned; bench window week of 2026-05-25.

Notes on transcription: Some names may be mis-labeled in parts; timestamps approximate.
